content: Electronic mosquito repellents (EMRs) are devices that are marketed with the claim of preventing mosquito bites and reducing the risk of malaria infection. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether EMRs are effective in preventing mosquito bites and to determine if there is any evidence supporting their impact on malaria infection. In March 2009, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, Cambridge Scientific Abstracts, and the Science Citation Index. Additional efforts included reviewing conference proceedings, contacting international specialist centers and EMR manufacturers, and examining reference lists for relevant studies. The selection criteria for this review included field entomological studies that controlled for variables such as geographic location, time, and the attractiveness of human participants to mosquitoes. Additionally, randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials assessing the efficacy of EMRs in preventing malaria infection were sought. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials, extracted the data, and performed the analysis. A total of ten field entomological studies met the inclusion criteria. All ten studies consistently demonstrated that there was no difference in the number of mosquitoes landing on the exposed skin of human participants, regardless of whether an EMR was used or not. Furthermore, no randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials evaluating the effectiveness of EMRs in preventing malaria infection were identified. The authors concluded that field entomological studies provide clear evidence that EMRs do not prevent mosquito bites. Consequently, there is no scientific basis to support the marketing of these devices as a means to prevent malaria infection.
